title: The Strategy Process
hook: Market maps look strategic until nobody can name the first profitable customer.
counterintuition: The destination gets the credit, but the real strategy is the how that survives customers, competition, capability, milestones, and economics.
tryThisNow: Take one strategic claim. Add the customer and competitor. Then add the profit path, milestone, and capability that would make it true.
keyTakeaway: A strategy earns belief when it explains how the business will win, execute, make money, and balance near-term work with long-term health.

breakdown.fastRead:
Oksana holds a curling market map while no one can name the customer who will buy first at a profit. The target is bold, but the path has not earned belief.

Turn strategy into a tested path. Ask which buyer matters, who can block you, which skill must exist, which next marker proves progress, and how the money works. A bold aim can excite a room. Strategy begins when the room can explain how the business will make the promise work.
breakdown.deepRead:
At 12:21 p.m., Hamza watches a founder point to a new segment on a slide while sales has no buyer name for it. The segment is a wish until the team can say why a real customer switches and how profit appears.

You can see the mechanism in the first awkward pause. People tend to protect a promise after it has been spoken out loud. They smooth bad news, widen dates, and call vague ownership teamwork. Making strategy prove how it will win, grow, execute, and make money cuts through that comfort by asking for the live fact that changes action.

At 4:14 p.m., Rhea sees a competitor's price sheet beside her own growth plan and realizes the plan never named the response. The useful move is not louder pressure. It is closer contact with the work. Ask who owns the next hard move, what might block it, and what proof will be visible soon. Then stay long enough to change the plan when the answer is rough.

At 9:29 a.m., Plinio asks for the operations capacity behind a strategic bet and hears silence after the word eventually. There is a limit. Strong execution cannot make a weak premise true. It can only expose the weak premise early, while a leader still has time to change the promise, move the person, narrow the goal, or stop pretending.
breakdown.fullRead:
Oksana stands in front of the market map and asks for the first profitable customer. The room has a growth target, a channel idea, and a clean slide on opportunity. What it does not have is a customer whose behavior, price, route cost, and timing make the plan real.

The strategy process starts with the hows. Where is the external environment moving? Which customers and markets are actually being served? Who is the competition? What is the best way to grow profitably? Can the business execute this strategy with the people and operations it has, or with the capability it can build in time?

Those questions are not consultant decoration. They are the difference between ambition and strategy. A regional soccer academy cannot call winter futsal a strategy while rival clubs own the gym slots. A cosmetics maker cannot call pharmacies a channel strategy while the batch-testing lab is already at capacity. A ferry authority cannot hide vessel replacement risk under short-term timetable fixes and pretend the long-term balance has been handled.

Milestones matter because they force time into the plan. A milestone should prove more than activity. It should show whether a customer has been reached, a capability has been built, a competitive response has been answered, or an economic assumption still holds. Without those tests, the plan can keep sounding strategic while it avoids the conditions that would make it true.

Sustainable economics are the hard check. A subscription can have interest and still fail after accreditation costs. A pickup service can attract attention and still lose money on route density. A nonprofit can promise job placements and still lack the employer partnerships needed to deliver them. The question is not whether the goal is worthy. The question is whether the plan can make money, serve people, or deliver outcomes on a sustainable basis.

There is a healthy discomfort in this process. It can feel like the questions are slowing momentum. In reality, they are protecting the organization from spending momentum on a story. Good strategy narrows. It chooses. It names what has to be true and what will be abandoned if those conditions fail.

Take one strategic claim and ask for the how in five places: customer, competition, capability, milestone, and economics. If the answer is thin in any one place, the strategy is still asking reality to wait.

A destination without a how is only a confident sentence.

A good strategy process should make the plan less comfortable and more useful. It may cut a market, delay a launch, narrow a customer segment, or expose a capability gap the team hoped to solve later. That is not failure. That is strategy becoming honest before operations has to pay for the fantasy.

The same pressure should reach every attractive idea. If the customer is vague, name the first buyer. If the capability is thin, name the build. If the economics are weak, change the offer before the market does it for you.

examples.title: Oksana asks for the first profitable customer

planSpec.domain: a strategy lead testing a market expansion claim against customer economics
planSpec.audience: a leader with a broad growth target and no first customer named
planSpec.stakes: a costly expansion into a market the company may not serve profitably
planSpec.requiredBeat: she asks for the first profitable customer while the map is still on the table

examples.scenario: At 8:08 a.m., Oksana smooths a curling market map on the boardroom table with the heel of her hand. The shaded region for commercial kitchens looks huge. The room likes the number. A coffee ring cuts across three counties. Oksana asks who the first profitable customer is, not the tenth, not the total market. The sales lead looks down at his binder. She is about to decide whether the expansion is a strategy or only a large colored shape.
examples.whatToDo: Hold the market claim until the team names the first buyer, the reason that buyer switches, and the margin after service costs.
examples.whyItMatters: A market size number can flatter a weak plan. Strategy starts where a real customer, competitor, and profit path meet.

examples.title: Hamza stops at the unnamed buyer

planSpec.domain: an investor pressing a founder on a new customer segment
planSpec.audience: a strategist who needs customer reality under growth language
planSpec.stakes: funding a plan with no proven switching reason
planSpec.requiredBeat: he asks why a named buyer would switch now

examples.scenario: "Which buyer switches first?" Hamza asks in the demo room while the enterprise expansion slide glows behind him. "Which buyer switches first?" he asks. The founder says, "Mid-market operations teams." Hamza waits. The projector fan rattles. "Name one," he says. The founder turns to the sales VP. Outside the glass, two engineers are watching. Hamza has to decide whether the segment is evidence or a phrase with a budget request attached.
examples.whatToDo: Ask for a named buyer, the pain that makes switching urgent, and the sales motion that has already tested that claim.
examples.whyItMatters: A customer segment is not a customer. Strategy needs a switching reason that can be heard from a real buyer.

examples.title: Rhea lays the competitor price sheet over the plan

planSpec.domain: a consumer-goods strategist testing a growth plan against competitor pricing
planSpec.audience: a leader whose plan ignores the rival response
planSpec.stakes: margin loss and a launch that may be copied in two weeks
planSpec.requiredBeat: she must decide whether to approve a plan that never named the competitor's likely move

examples.scenario: The competitor price sheet lands over Rhea's growth plan and the paper edges line up almost perfectly. The new bundle wins only if the rival does not answer for ninety days. Last quarter the rival answered in twelve. The launch team is waiting for approval, pizza boxes open on the credenza. Rhea's pen rests on the signature line. She must decide whether a strategy that ignores the obvious response is ready.
examples.whatToDo: Send the plan back with a competitor-response section, including price floor, margin impact, and the trigger for changing the offer.
examples.whyItMatters: A strategy has to win against someone. If the competitor's likely move breaks the economics, the plan is only a hope.

examples.title: Plinio hears eventually after asking about capacity

planSpec.domain: an operations chief reviewing a strategic bet that lacked carrying capacity
planSpec.audience: a leader who heard future capability used as proof
planSpec.stakes: missed delivery after a strategic promise outran the operation
planSpec.requiredBeat: she identifies the moment capacity was waved away

examples.scenario: It takes Plinio until 9:29 a.m. in the rollout postmortem, with a yellow legal pad open, to hear the word eventually as a warning. In the recording, he hears himself ask who would install the new units. Someone answered, "We'll build that capacity eventually." He let the word pass. Now two customers are waiting, the installer bench is empty, and the pad smells of fresh ink. Plinio circles eventually until the paper dents.
examples.whatToDo: Make capacity a gate for strategic approval: named roles, hiring or training path, and milestone evidence before volume promises expand.
examples.whyItMatters: Future capacity cannot carry current strategy. The how must include the people and operating path that make growth possible.

examples.title: Wren erases the growth curve on the glass

planSpec.domain: a manufacturing strategist replacing a smooth growth curve with milestones
planSpec.audience: a leader who needs proof points under a growth story
planSpec.stakes: adding a second shift without economic proof
planSpec.requiredBeat: he changes the strategy from curve to testable milestones

examples.scenario: What happens at 6:52 p.m. in the conference room when Wren's rising growth curve meets the scheduler's second-shift roster on the glass? Before the scheduler arrived, the curve made the growth plan feel clean. After she asks which week demand pays for the shift premium, Wren stops with the marker in midair. He wipes the curve into a gray smear and writes three dates instead: pilot orders, margin check, second-shift call.
examples.whatToDo: Replace the smooth curve with milestones that test demand, margin, and capacity before the second shift is locked.
examples.whyItMatters: Milestones make strategy answer reality in sequence. A curve can hide the week when economics must prove themselves.

examples.title: Beata reads strategy from the complaint log

planSpec.domain: a service strategist using customer complaints to test a market need
planSpec.audience: a strategist tempted by polished market language
planSpec.stakes: choosing a growth direction that may miss the customer's real pain
planSpec.requiredBeat: she finds the real strategic need in rough customer language

examples.scenario: You smell lemon cleaner on the conference table as Beata opens the customer complaint log. The strategy deck says integrated convenience. The complaints say missed pickup windows, wet boxes, no one called me back. She reads six in a row and feels the deck language loosen. The market is not asking for elegance. It is asking not to be stranded on Tuesdays. Beata copies one raw sentence into the plan.
examples.whatToDo: Translate the strategy around the customer's real pain, then test whether the company can solve that pain better than the alternatives.
examples.whyItMatters: Customer reality gives strategy its shape. Polished language can miss the job the buyer is actually trying to get done.

reviewCards.front: A plan sounds clear, but the next hard owner is unnamed. What should you retrieve?
reviewCards.back: Retrieve the execution test: name the owner, the next action, the date, and the evidence that will prove the work moved.

reviewCards.front: A team gives calm status while field evidence feels rough. What move keeps truth close?
reviewCards.back: Ask for the raw signal from the place where the work happens, then decide what changes before the next review.

reviewCards.front: You spot a comforting story covering a weak handoff. What question breaks the spell?
reviewCards.back: Ask what must be true by a near date, who owns that proof, and what will happen if the proof does not appear.

reviewCards.front: A target was built on a false assumption. What does strong follow-through require?
reviewCards.back: Change the target, name the failed premise, and protect the system from pretending the old promise still fits reality.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: making strategy prove how it will win, grow, execute, and make money starts with a live promise and forces it into owned action. The habit is to ask what is true now, who owns the next hard move, and what proof will appear soon.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a work plan earns quick agreement, then I will ask for the owner, date, and proof point on the hardest piece before I call it ready.
If I set a health goal, then I will name the next physical setup, the time it happens, and the check I will use tomorrow.
If I keep repeating a personal promise, then I will turn it into one visible action with a time, place, and fallback.
If someone depends on me, then I will state exactly what I will do next and when they can see or hear the result.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, choose one promise that sounds settled and write the owner, the next action, the riskiest assumption, and the proof you expect to see within seven days.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, end each serious planning conversation by asking what changed, who owns the next hard move, and what evidence will be visible before the next check-in.
